title: The world's biggest dinner party comes to Shenzhen: 37 years ago, 12 'brothers' got together and were laughed out of town; today 21 economies are fighting for a seat at the table
summary: The whole world is flying to Shenzhen: the CEO Summit and Leaders' Meeting take the stage back to back, and the 'Shenzhen Initiative' becomes the first outcome document issued in initiative form in 30 years. Here's a plain-language walk through APEC's past and present — from 12 economies in Canberra in 1989 to 21 today.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: This week, the busiest people on the planet are all flying to Shenzhen. On November 18, the APEC CEO Summit opened at the Qianhai International Convention Center; on November 19, the 33rd Leaders' Non-formal Meeting took the baton. Heads of state and global business heavyweights are lining up to make an appearance.

The mechanism known by the acronym APEC turns 37 this year. When it was born in 1989, plenty of people were waiting for a good laugh: a bunch of Pacific Rim countries gathering for meetings with no binding rules and no enforcement power — wasn't it just a chat club?

Well, that 'chat club' talked its way to 21 members, to half of the Asia-Pacific's economic growth, and all the way to Shenzhen in 2026. Today we'll use plain language to run through the past and present of the world's biggest dinner party.
◆ Prologue: This week, the whole world is flying to Shenzhen

During the day on November 18, the CEO Summit opened with round after round of applause in the hall; that evening, a state banquet at the Shenzhen International Exchange Center welcomed leaders from all countries gathered under one roof. This is the third time China has hosted APEC, after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.

And they dropped a big one that same day: the '2026 APEC CEO Summit Shenzhen Initiative' was released, the first time in the CEO Summit's 30-year history that an outcome document took the form of an initiative. It calls for deepening an open regional economy and driving inclusive growth through technological innovation.

Australia's leader Anthony Albanese mused that if you put photos of Shenzhen from 1998 and 2026 side by side, you'd never believe it was the same place. The Guardian put it even more directly: there's no better stage than Shenzhen for telling the Asia-Pacific story.
◆ Birth: Canberra 1989, the gathering of 12 'brothers'

Rewind to the start of 1989. In a speech in Seoul, then-Australian leader Bob Hawke threw out the idea: the economies around the Pacific Rim should sit down at one table and talk business. More than a few newspapers treated it as a joke over tea.

Yet on November 5–7, 1989, Canberra actually pulled it off: Australia, the United States, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand and Canada, plus the six ASEAN countries — 12 members in all — held the first Ministerial Meeting, and APEC was officially open for business.

A humble start, with simple rules: no hard contracts, no fixed deadlines, anyone free to talk with anyone. Who could have imagined that this loose, makeshift outfit would grow into the highest-level, broadest economic cooperation mechanism in the Asia-Pacific?
◆ Childhood: Seattle 1993, a leather jacket sets the tone

In November 1993, then-US leader Bill Clinton rounded up the bigwigs and brought them to Blake Island near Seattle for the first Leaders' Non-formal Meeting. Suits and ties were out; slip on a leather jacket and the whole thing suddenly felt right.

The word 'non-formal' became APEC's soul from then on: however lofty your title, once you're on the island you leave your airs at the door and actually talk. That same year, the APEC Secretariat set up home in Singapore — the organization finally had a place to call its own.
From 1993 on, the Leaders' Non-formal Meeting became an annual fixture, usually held between September and November, and it hasn't missed a year since.
◆ Growing up: Bogor 1994, setting the alarm clock for globalization

In 1994, the meeting moved to Bogor, Indonesia, giving us the Bogor Goals: developed members would achieve trade and investment liberalization by 2010, developing members by 2020. It was a hard alarm clock for the whole Asia-Pacific's opening-up process.

The 1995 Osaka Action Agenda followed, setting two wheels in motion: trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, and economic and technical cooperation. The 1996 Subic Bay meeting in the Philippines added another stroke: voluntary action and consensus — nobody gets to strong-arm anyone with a memo. APEC's character was set right there.
The 1997 Vancouver meeting expanded the club, with Vietnam, Russia and Peru joining one after another. The table got bigger and the menu got longer.
◆ China enters the stage: Shanghai 2001, the tang-suit group photo

2001 was a year of double celebrations: China hosted the APEC Leaders' Non-formal Meeting in Shanghai for the first time, and joined the World Trade Organization the same year. Old hands all knew the two were part of the same game plan.

That year's group photo in matching tang suits is still an iconic scene: leaders of the 21 economies dressed alike, and traditional Chinese elements grabbed global headlines for the first time. The meeting also produced the Shanghai Consensus to accelerate the Bogor Goals.

Over the next 25 years, China fully honored its WTO commitments, making its 'list of opportunities' longer and longer. Hosting again in 2026 was a third time at the bat — and a banquet brought back to its own home.
◆ Highlight: Beijing 2014, Yanqi Lake and the connectivity blueprint

In 2014, APEC came home — by Yanqi Lake in Beijing, the meeting adopted the Beijing Framework and a statement marking 25 years of APEC, focusing on regional economic integration, innovative growth and connectivity.

The light show at Yanqi Lake fed the world's cameras to their fill. More important was the substance: the FTAAP process moved forward in real terms, the connectivity blueprint took shape, and infrastructure, policy and people-to-people ties were all laid out together.

In the years that followed, Manila talked inclusion, Lima talked growth, Da Nang talked micro, small and medium enterprises — the seed of the FTAAP was passed along from hand to hand, and it's still sprouting in Shenzhen today.
◆ Rough seas: 2019 cancelled, 2020 online — the family doesn't break up

APEC has had its share of scares too. In 2019, host Chile abruptly cancelled the Leaders' Meeting because of domestic unrest, and many thought the year would be a blank — but the Senior Officials' Meeting went ahead as usual at the Singapore secretariat, with not a single roadmap missing.

Then the pandemic hit in 2020. Malaysia moved the meeting onto video links and online adopted the Putrajaya Vision 2040: building an open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040. They couldn't meet in person, but not a word of the conversation was lost.

In 2021 New Zealand hosted two video meetings in one year, and in 2023 everyone sat down at the same table again in San Francisco. Over 37 years the dinner party has had its awkward silences, but it has never broken up — that's the toughest skill in this group chat of friends.
◆ Where things stand: 21 members and the 2026 Shenzhen report card

Today's APEC has 21 members stretching across the Asia-Pacific: China, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Russia, Australia... including Hong Kong, China and Chinese Taipei, plus three observers such as the ASEAN Secretariat. More than half of the region's total economic output sits at this table.

The 2025 Gyeongju meeting had just adopted the APEC AI Initiative, and Shenzhen in 2026 took the baton and raised the stakes: China announced US$20 million to fund practical cooperation, the establishment of an Asia-Pacific Community Research Center in Shenzhen, and support for setting up a World Bay Area Economic Cooperation Alliance.

The report card is solid too: China's economy grew 4.6% in the first three quarters, and Shenzhen is the perfect case study of the Asia-Pacific growth story. To sum up the 2026 home game: playing host, footing the bill, providing the platform — nothing missing.
◆ In closing: Pengcheng, a journey of a thousand miles

Shenzhen is also known as Pengcheng, the City of the Roc. The parting blessing from the Chinese side at the meeting was a fine one: may Asia-Pacific cooperation spread its wings like the great roc and soar a thousand miles.

Looking back over 37 years, APEC's secret of success is almost charmingly simple: no cliques, no blacklists, no table-flipping at the drop of a hat — just talk things through slowly and do business in earnest.

From the humble beginnings of 12 'brothers' in Canberra to a full-blown feast for 21 economies on the shores of Shenzhen Bay, this world's biggest dinner party proves one thing: openness is the base code of Asia-Pacific prosperity.
The dinner party goes on, and we'll be following the story at the next stop.
Add up these 37 years and you'll find APEC's most mesmerizing trick: it forces nothing, yet it's stirred up business across half the globe into a boiling pot.

The people who laughed in 1989 are long silent; today economies line up to grab the head seat. The organization doesn't care how humble your start was — it cares whether you can keep your seat at the table.
Shenzhen 2026 added a new footnote to this dinner party: tell the story through bay areas, trade openness for growth, and simmer an Asia-Pacific miracle over 37 patient years.
As for who hosts next and what new dishes will come out of the conversation, we'll just have to wait and see.
This article draws on public reports from Xinhua, the APEC official website and other sources.

title: That 1989 dinner party nobody believed in: 12 economies were mocked as a talking shop; 37 years later, 21 are fighting for the head table
summary: That 1989 dinner party nobody believed in: 12 economies were mocked as a talking shop; 37 years later, 21 are fighting for the head table. Hawke's call in Seoul, ASEAN's rules as a protective charm, the humble opening in Canberra — the full birth certificate is right here.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: When you think of an international organization, you probably picture suits, simultaneous-translation headsets and endless communiqués. The 1989 meeting in Canberra started just as humbly — many media outlets around the world gave it barely more column inches than an obituary. Nobody expected this loose dinner party, mocked as a talking shop, to grow into a superclub of 3 billion people with 60% of global GDP.

Today the APEC website posts some hard numbers: 21 members, about 3 billion people or 36.4% of the world, and a combined GDP of US$61.4 trillion, or 61.6% of the global total — as if half the globe's business had been packed onto a single table.
This article digs up its birth certificate — one so earnest it's almost funny, and one that has decided the wallets of billions.
◆ A scattered Asia-Pacific in need of a table

In the late 1980s, the Asia-Pacific economy was red hot: the Four Asian Tigers were spreading factories around the world, and Japanese cars and home appliances were conquering markets. Japan sat firmly as the world's second-largest economy, while exports from South Korea and Taiwan region were climbing by double digits year after year, and economists worldwide cried that the Pacific Century had arrived.

The awkward part: the whole Asia-Pacific didn't even have a decent economic coordination mechanism; cooperation basically ran on bilateral talks and informal consultation. Meanwhile Europeans were building the European Community, and North America was quietly negotiating a free-trade deal. Over here around the Pacific, all we had were academic salons and semi-official forums to keep up appearances.

And trade wars poured fuel on the fire: after the 1985 Plaza Accord the yen was forced up, US-Japan semiconductor talks went tit for tat, and the Uruguay Round launched in 1986 collapsed several times over several years. Everyone's temper was at a boiling point. Business across the Pacific kept growing, but the table for arguing kept shrinking.

One media outlet quipped that Asia-Pacific economic cooperation was like a country fair: everyone sells their own wares, and arguments are settled by who shouts loudest. Harsh words, but close to the truth — the scattered Asia-Pacific really was missing a table to sit down at.
◆ Hawke's call from Seoul

On January 31, 1989, then-Australian leader Bob Hawke publicly floated a bold idea in Seoul: the major Asia-Pacific economies should sit down and hold a regular ministerial meeting. The union-born leader delivered the proposal as crisply as if he were announcing a game schedule.

The moment the proposal landed, embassies were telegraphing late into the night. Some worried about domination by the US, Japan and Australia; some feared it would turn into an all-talk club; there were even rumors that the big powers only wanted a small exclusive circle. Gossip flew everywhere, and most people sat on the fence.

But Hawke bet on the right moment: the Uruguay Round deadlock had made countries realize that if global multilateral talks stalled, they needed a backup at the regional level. Everyone wanted a table where they could argue and do business — all that was missing was someone brave enough to speak first.

Even smarter was the choice of Seoul — launching the initiative in the heart of Asia was a statement on the spot: this isn't an Anglo club, it's a dinner party for the whole Asia-Pacific. A play on timing and a play on positioning — the veteran politician's touch was all over that speech.
◆ ASEAN takes the head seat: looseness is the protective charm

The toughest hurdle was ASEAN. The six ASEAN countries — Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Brunei — had butterflies: a regional organization was fine, but if the US, Japan and Australia ran the show, wouldn't the leading roles become supporting ones? That worry nearly killed the dinner party on the spot.

So the rules followed ASEAN's habits: no binding treaties, no hard thresholds, everything by consensus, voluntary and flexible, step by step. This design, jokingly called the least bossy around, became the core code that kept APEC alive for 37 years — no member could use it to force another member's hand.

ASEAN also secured the arrangements for observers and the secretariat: at the 1989 meeting, ASEAN countries held half of the 12 founding seats; the secretariat landed in Singapore in 1993, and at every meeting since, ASEAN has kept the seat of honor.

Looseness, precisely, was the charm. History has repeatedly shown since: the more tightly an international organization is run, the faster it falls apart, while APEC, powered by a spirit of 'let's talk it over,' managed to extend its life to 37 years.
◆ Canberra opens: the first table of 12

On November 5–7, 1989, the first Ministerial Meeting opened in Canberra. Australia, the United States, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand, plus the six ASEAN countries — all 12 founding members present. No earth-shattering treaty; the agenda was as plain as a neighborhood committee's: meet, get acquainted, and set the rules for where to hold the next one.

The joint statement released was a few thin pages, with one core line: the Asia-Pacific needs regular economic consultation. Even the organization's name was settled on the spot — the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Conference, renamed Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in 1993. About as unglamorous as it gets, but it worked.
Even the following year's schedule was decided on the spot: Singapore would host in 1990, then Bangkok and Seoul would take turns. One rotation table beats ten pages of bylaws.

Yet it was this plain meeting that, for the first time, put the decades-scattered Asia-Pacific economies into the same room — and the biggest blank spot on the global trade map was filled from then on.
◆ Expansion is like opening blind boxes, and the seats keep filling up

Once the dinner party started, good news traveled fast. In November 1991, the third Ministerial Meeting in Seoul, South Korea issued three new tickets: China joined as a sovereign state, while Chinese Taipei and Hong Kong took seats at the same time as regional economies. The table grew from 12 to 15 — the Asia-Pacific's heaviest-weight markets finally sat together.

From 1993 to 1994, Mexico, Papua New Guinea and Chile joined in succession; in 1998 Peru, Russia and Vietnam took their places, and the full 21-member lineup took shape. No further expansion in the 28 years since — not because nobody wanted in, but because the seats really were full.

Look at the economic miracles on this membership list: the rise of Taipei 101, the neon of Seoul, the containers on Singapore's docks, Shenzhen's transformation from fishing village to tech hub — all of it happened on APEC's table.

The official website lists the 21 members' assets at a glance: GDP of US$61.4 trillion, or 61.6% of the world; merchandise exports and imports of about US$15.3 trillion each, each nearly half the global total — the snowball started rolling the moment China joined in 1991.
◆ The talking shop's comeback

More than 30 years on, the talking shop once mocked as nothing but tea and chatter has become the highest-level, broadest and most influential economic cooperation mechanism in the Asia-Pacific: from one ministerial meeting to more than twenty, with ministers for trade, finance, energy and food security clocking in year after year.

It still signs no binding treaties, running on a group photo and a declaration, yet it has genuinely lifted the Asia-Pacific into the engine room of the global economy, with exports and imports of about US$15.3 trillion each, nearly half the world's total; and the secretariat has even raised the region's 2026 growth forecast to 3.4%.

Not to mention the chain of outcomes it has hatched: the Leaders' Non-formal Meeting, the Bogor Goals, the FTAAP roadmap, the 2040 Vision — an organization once mocked as a talking shop actually set the Asia-Pacific's agenda for three decades.
By now you'll have noticed: a low bar isn't a lack of ability — it's a higher way of living.
That 1989 dinner party nobody believed in is now a card table for 60% of global GDP: 3 billion people, US$61.4 trillion in economic output, and nearly half of the world's imports and exports.
History proves again and again: getting people together matters more than nailing down the rules first.
Next time someone says international organizations are all talk, just toss them APEC's birth certificate.
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.

title: From 12 to 21: APEC's 37 years have been like opening blind boxes — China joined in 1991, and the 2001 group photo switched to tang suits
summary: From 12 to 21: APEC's 37 years have been like opening blind boxes — China joined in 1991, ties came off in Seattle in 1993, the alarm clock was set in Bogor in 1994, and the 2001 group photo switched to tang suits. Every upgrade hit the rhythm of the times.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: How does an international organization with no treaty constraints and no punishment mechanism survive to 37 and keep getting stronger? The answer lies in its history: every expansion and upgrade caught the rhythm of the times, growing from a ministers' club into a heads-of-state dinner party.

Its filing cabinet is full of iconic scenes: ties off in Seattle in 1993, the alarm clock set in Bogor in 1994, China joining in 1991, tang suits in Shanghai in 2001, the Yanqi Lake blueprint in 2014, the Shenzhen report card in 2026 — every step landed right where the global economy was shifting gears.
This piece walks you through it on a timeline, showing exactly where every step from 12 to 21 was taken.
◆ Canberra opening: the ministers' club era

The first Ministerial Meeting in 1989 had only 12 members, with an agenda of meeting, getting acquainted and setting rules. The second went to Singapore the next year, then Bangkok in 1991 and Seoul in 1992 — in its first four years, the ministerial meeting turned the rotation schedule into a tradition.

Early APEC was a pure ministers' club, with no leaders in the room, permanently at the bottom of the media heat charts, the least eye-catching paragraph in any press release. Even members admitted that its biggest achievement in those years was getting everyone used to meeting once a year.
But habit is an asset: four meetings in four years, and the prototype of the secretariat, the rules of rotation, and the consensus-building style all quietly took shape during this overlooked window.
Nobody expected that a move by a US leader in 1993 would lift it straight into the headlines of great-power rivalry.
◆ 1991: China joins, and the table really starts turning

In November 1991, the third Ministerial Meeting was held in Seoul. China formally joined as a sovereign state, while Chinese Taipei and Hong Kong took seats at the same time as regional economies. The Asia-Pacific's heaviest-weight markets finally sat at the same table.

The weight of this step was visible right away: China, Japan, the United States and ASEAN — the world's factory, the biggest consumer market and the largest transshipment hub appeared together for the first time, and overnight APEC went from a regional club to the main artery of global trade.

Its long-term payoff only fully arrived a decade later: China joined the WTO in December 2001, just after Shanghai hosted APEC that October — two celebrations in one year, with the host role serving as the best dress rehearsal for WTO entry.
From then on APEC's ledger read: 21 members, about 3 billion people, 61.6% of global GDP — the numbers posted on the official website started snowballing from that year.
◆ Seattle debut: the leaders take off their ties

In November 1993, Clinton invited the leaders of member economies to Blake Island near Seattle for the first Leaders' Non-formal Meeting. The word 'non-formal' in the name basically meant: no ties, fewer scripts, more plain talking — not even a head seat at the table, so nobody could put on airs.

That year's meeting pledged to deepen the spirit of the Asia-Pacific family and to secure stability, security and prosperity for the region's peoples, and the annual leaders' gathering became a fixed program from then on. The media discovered for the first time that watching great-power leaders chat without a script was a lot more interesting than reading a statement.
How clever was the 'non-formal' design? It sidestepped the rigid protocols of officialdom: no treaty, no votes, just frank conversation around the fire — looser in form, heavier in substance.
APEC officially graduated from a ministers' club to a heads-of-state dinner party — and as its stature rose, the global spotlight followed.
◆ Bogor sets the goals: an alarm clock for liberalization

November 15, 1994, Bogor, Indonesia. In a mountain retreat, 21 members set an absurdly ambitious goal: developed members would achieve trade and investment liberalization by 2010, developing members by 2020. This was the Bogor Goals, straight into the textbooks — the first time the Asia-Pacific's opening-up process was wound up like a clock.

The media did the math on the spot: this ambition outstripped even the European Community, and waves of doubt followed. But it was precisely this declaration that twisted the loose dinner party into a single rope: with goals and deadlines on the table, nobody could hedge anymore.

Supporting mechanisms followed closely: the 1995 Osaka meeting adopted the Osaka Action Agenda, breaking the goals into specific sectors; the 1996 Subic meeting produced Individual Action Plans, with each member reporting its own progress and airing its own commitments — handing in homework to themselves.

By 2020, average import tariffs across the Asia-Pacific had fallen from double digits in the late 1980s to single digits, and trade costs dropped sharply — the alarm clock had rung, and its chime turned into hard cash.
◆ Expanding through the financial storm: what a tough life force

The 1997 Asian financial storm struck, and the Thai baht was halved overnight: on July 2 it abandoned its fixed exchange rate; within months the rupiah, won and ringgit took turns plunging, stock markets cratered in several countries, and IMF bailout packages were negotiated round after round.

In the middle of this mess, the November 1997 Vancouver meeting still expanded: it announced the admission of Vietnam, Russia and Peru, all in place by 1998. Handing in a pledge of allegiance in a crisis year was a bet that the Asia-Pacific must stay open for the long haul — the bigger the storm, the sturdier the table.

The 1998 Kuala Lumpur meeting went ahead under the storm: host Malaysia had imposed capital controls in September and openly stood up to the IMF, and the meeting also saw the furor over a speech by second-in-command Al Gore — the explosive atmosphere of that session is still dinner-table talk for veteran negotiators.
The crisis didn't break up the dinner party; instead it expanded the membership and set a social safety net and cooperation agenda — that's just how tough this organization is.
◆ Shanghai's tang-suit group photo: China's home-court year one

October 20–21, 2001, Shanghai. Only a month after 9/11, with global security tensions running high, APEC went ahead as scheduled — China's first time as host, and one of the heaviest gatherings on the Asia-Pacific multilateral calendar after 9/11. Leaders from various countries put on tang suits for a group photo that went into the history books.

The results were solid too: the Shanghai Consensus, the e-APEC Strategy and a leaders' counter-terrorism statement filled a whole page — the digital agenda hit the table for the first time, planting the seeds for two decades of paperless trade and the e-commerce boom.

Thirteen years later came Yanqi Lake in Beijing, with the connectivity blueprint and the FTAAP roadmap landing in a big way; another twelve years on, it was Shenzhen's turn — three home games in 25 years, and China answered the host question three different ways.
From tidal-flat fishing village to city of technology, the growth rings of the host city are the growth rings of APEC.
Thirty-seven years, 12 to 21 people, ministers' meetings turned into heads-of-state meetings, a loose dinner party turned into a council for 60% of global GDP.
APEC's history proves one thing over and over: slow is fast; scattered but not chaotic.
The next chapter is Shenzhen's turn to hold the pen.
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.

title: Shenzhen is hosting the world's most expensive meeting: US$20 million in cold hard cash, and an Asia-Pacific Community Research Center settling in Pengcheng today
summary: US$20 million in real money, an Asia-Pacific Community Research Center landing in Pengcheng, and a World Bay Area Economic Cooperation Alliance: the 2026 Shenzhen Summit tightened a notch on the loose mechanism, on top of a report card covering 60% of global GDP.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: These days the world's eyes are squeezing into a southern city. In November 2026, the 33rd APEC Leaders' Non-formal Meeting is underway in Shenzhen: the CEO Summit on the 18th, the Leaders' Meeting on the 19th — a schedule fuller than the Spring Festival travel rush.

This is China's third time as host — Shanghai in 2001, Beijing in 2014, Shenzhen in 2026, three straight terms in 25 years. Let's take stock: what big moves were announced in the hall, and just how daunting this Asia-Pacific report card is.

First, a string of warm-up numbers: about 3 billion people, US$61.4 trillion in GDP, and roughly US$15.3 trillion each in imports and exports — the economic mass behind this meeting accounts for 60% of the world.
◆ Pengcheng right now: the world's hottest meeting room

On the morning of November 18, the CEO Summit opened at the Qianhai International Convention Center; on the 19th, the 33rd Leaders' Non-formal Meeting took over. Global dignitaries, entrepreneurs and media crowded the shores of the South China Sea, with a theme summed up in one line: building an Asia-Pacific community and sharing a prosperous future.

This is China's third time hosting in APEC's 37 years, after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014 — one country running the Leaders' Meeting three times in 25 years is a first in the entire Asia-Pacific mechanism.

Choosing Qianhai as the venue was no accident: this stretch of reclaimed tidal flats is now the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Modern Service Industry Cooperation Zone, with tens of thousands of registered companies — bringing the global business community to meet in China's most economically active testing ground was itself an item on the agenda.
How hot was the atmosphere? Even hotel room rates and seats in the tech park cafés were making way for this meeting.
◆ Three home games, three report cards

Shanghai 2001, the tang-suit group photo, keywords: the eve of WTO entry and e-APEC. Beijing 2014, the Yanqi Lake blueprint, keywords: connectivity and the FTAAP roadmap. Shenzhen 2026, the bay-area report card, keywords: innovation and the Asia-Pacific community.

The three home games line up with three steps in China's economy: a debut on the eve of WTO entry, a banquet as the world's second-largest economy, and today's host of the digital and bay-area economy — the weight of the host is the weight of the nation.

Shenzhen's own résumé is equally hard-core: a border town of just over 30,000 people four decades ago, it now has nearly 18 million permanent residents and a regional GDP topping 3.6 trillion yuan. From small fishing village to city of innovation, it's a concentrated sample of the Asia-Pacific miracle.
Choosing this city as host was persuasive all by itself.
◆ Three moves with real money behind them

At the Leaders' Meeting on November 19, the Chinese side announced on the spot: US$20 million to fund practical APEC cooperation; the establishment of an Asia-Pacific Community Research Center in Shenzhen; and cooperation bodies in fields including digital technology, cross-border data flows, clean energy and small and medium enterprise development.

Break down the weight of each: the US$20 million is operating funds for a loose mechanism, the research center gives 37 years of experience intellectual backing, and the cooperation bodies in four fields turn declarations into schedules — money, think tank and levers, nothing missing.

Especially the move to put the research center in Shenzhen: after 37 years of Asia-Pacific cooperation, with practices, communiqués and roadmaps scattered across meeting documents, this is the first time a dedicated body will do systematic research and talent training — the equivalent of building this mechanism an archive plus a laboratory.
A mechanism loose for 37 years finally got a real gift package this time, and plenty of media used 'gift package' right in their headlines.
◆ The bay-area alliance: stringing the world's engines onto one line

Another low-key but subtle move was support for setting up a World Bay Area Economic Cooperation Alliance. New York, San Francisco, Tokyo, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area — for the first time, the world's top bay areas had a horizontal alliance, linking the showrooms of open economies into a network.

The numbers look good: the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao bay area has over 80 million permanent residents and an economic output approaching that of the New York bay area; Shenzhen alone regularly posts import-export totals that rival the national accounts of many small and medium economies — networking the bay areas means stringing half the world's innovation engines onto one line.

The essence of bay-area economy is openness, coordination and spillover: capital crosses bridges, talent commutes, technology scales walls. Once the alliance gets running, the redundancy and resilience of Asia-Pacific supply chains will step up a level.
The Shenzhen Bay Sports Center is shaped like a spring cocoon, and everyone has had lively fun interpreting the 'breaking out of the cocoon' meaning.
◆ The report card: a behemoth holding 60% of the world

Check a few of the latest figures on the APEC website: about 3 billion people, or 36.4% of the world; GDP of US$61.4 trillion, or 61.6% of the global total; merchandise exports and imports of about US$15.3 trillion each, accounting for 46.7% and 46.1% of the world respectively — nearly half of global goods trade runs across this table.

The growth curve is turning up too: on November 15, 2026, the APEC Policy Support Unit raised the regional growth forecast to 3.4% — in a year when protectionism is everywhere and major global institutions keep cutting their forecasts, this report card can more than hold its own.

A few more angles: the Asia-Pacific's near-half share of global trade means the chip in your phone, the clothes on your back and the cherries on your table most likely passed through an APEC member's port; average import tariffs among members have dropped sharply since the mechanism's early days.
The Asia-Pacific miracle isn't an adjective — it's an audited balance sheet.
◆ A thousand-mile flight: this city can handle it

The coastline at Dameisha is probably about to be photographed bald these days. Between sessions, dignitaries and entrepreneurs talk AI, cross-border data and green energy — one harder topic after another; on the CEO Summit's breakout session list, digital, green and small-business themes almost sweep the floor.

The Chinese side said in its speech: may Asia-Pacific cooperation spread its wings like the great roc and fly a thousand miles. Shenzhen is also called Pengcheng, the City of the Roc — those four characters fit this city like a glove.

For businesses and ordinary people, the most concrete expectations from this meeting come in three: smoother cross-border e-commerce rules, clear guidelines for data flows, and more cooperation channels for small businesses — the grand community narrative ultimately lands on customs declarations and logistics forms.
The closing of the meeting is only a comma — with the research center and cooperation bodies landing in Shenzhen, the second half of the story is just beginning.
US$20 million, one research center, a batch of cooperation bodies, one bay-area alliance — this Shenzhen meeting tightened a notch on the loose mechanism.
The card table for 60% of global GDP has moved into Pengcheng, and half the report card is already in.
The other half depends on how the next three years write it.
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.

title: APEC's most awkward moments: a meeting cancelled halfway through, the first stillborn communiqué in history, and a group photo that nearly didn't happen
summary: Cancelled halfway through by the host, the first stillborn joint declaration in history, a guest flipping the table on the spot: a look at APEC's most awkward moments, and why this 37-year-old mechanism comes through every time.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: When we talk about international organizations, everyone loves the highlight reels. But what really reveals a mechanism's true mettle is its darkest hours — a meeting cancelled halfway through by the host, the first stillborn joint declaration, a group photo that nearly didn't happen.

APEC has had every one of these awkward moments over 37 years: the table-flipping in Kuala Lumpur in 1998, the stillborn declaration in Port Moresby in 2018, the cancelled meeting in Santiago in 2019, the shadow over Da Nang in 2017. The amazing part: it came through every time, and grew stronger with every blow.
This piece deliberately picks the awkward moments — because a mechanism's true color shows not in fair winds, but against the wind.
◆ The Kuala Lumpur scene: the guest flips the host's table

Kuala Lumpur, November 1998, the financial storm's embers still glowing. Host Malaysia had imposed capital controls in September, acting unilaterally against International Monetary Fund pressure — practically a heretical move in the Western economics community of the time.

At the meeting, then-US number two Al Gore gave a speech publicly endorsing Malaysia's reformists — the host laid on the feast, and the guest flipped the table on the spot; the room froze in an instant: host Mahathir kept a stone face throughout, and the next day's meeting schedule went ahead anyway. That scene became the most famous awkward moment in APEC history.

But the meeting still finished, the declaration still went out, and nobody walked out. Capital controls were later even shown to be effective in stabilizing the local currency — the two table-flippers didn't fall out before finishing the meal.
Lesson one at the negotiating table: awkwardness doesn't kill you; breaking up does.
◆ Port Moresby: the first stillbirth in history

Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea, November 2018: trade friction between two major powers hit its peak, and 21 members argued over the declaration text down to the last minute — for the first time in the history of the Leaders' Meeting, there was no joint declaration, only a host's statement. In 37 years, the communiqué had handed in a blank paper for the first time.

Delegations from several countries later revealed that the split was over the wording on the multilateral trading system: one side wanted 'oppose protectionism,' the other insisted on 'unfair trade practices' — a few adjectives' difference kept 21 delegations rewriting drafts all night.

Even more surreal was what happened offstage: the two countries' negotiating teams kept trading blows on nearby ships — tit for tat on the flagship's deck, while inside the venue people shook hands and posed for photos as usual. However fierce the argument, not a day of business stopped.
Reporters rewrote their copy again and again, and in the end there was only one word left in the headline: 'rare.'
◆ Santiago: the meeting that vanished halfway through

Chile was due to host in 2019, but domestic unrest escalated in October, and then-Chilean leader Sebastián Piñera announced on October 30 the cancellation of that year's Leaders' Meeting — a first in APEC history. Flights were booked and bags were packed, and the Asia-Pacific's biggest year-end dinner party just disappeared.

For a while, everyone worried the mechanism would break up right there, with one comment flatly stating: the alarm bell has rung for Asia-Pacific cooperation. After all, without leaders backing it, the whole year's agenda had lost its main pillar.

As it turned out, in December the Senior Officials' Meeting wrapped up as usual at the Singapore secretariat, with roadmaps on marine debris and fighting illegal fishing all intact; in 2020 Malaysia took over and moved the Leaders' Meeting onto video — the meeting was gone, but the work never stopped, not a single task lost.

This lesson is about the value of redundancy: a rotation system plus a permanent secretariat amounts to a spare tire fitted to the mechanism — even with the host absent, the steering wheel still turns.
◆ Two years held up by video meetings

The pandemic arrived in 2020, and Malaysia moved the Leaders' Meeting onto video, releasing the weighty Putrajaya Vision 2040: an open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040 — a plan for the next twenty years delivered in a pandemic year, its value seriously underestimated.

New Zealand went further in 2021, holding two video Leaders' Meetings in a single year: July set the agenda for pandemic cooperation and economic recovery, and November nailed down the Aotearoa Action Plan, breaking the 2040 Vision into assessable blueprints.

Two years without a group photo, without handshakes and pictures, without banquets and state gifts — and not a single item missing from the results list, with the agenda advancing even faster than in some face-to-face years.
The two years without a group photo actually produced two hard-core documents — proof that taking pictures was never this organization's main business.
◆ The shadow over Da Nang: the multilateral table keeps turning

Da Nang, November 2017: the new US administration announced its withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership — a multilateral free-trade agreement whose negotiations were launched by APEC members, and now its initiator was walking away at the eleventh hour. The FTAAP roadmap was instantly cast in shadow, and outsiders wondered whether this meeting would turn into a trap.

As it turned out, the leaders' declaration went out as usual, inclusive growth and MSME issues were pushed as usual, and food security and digital trade agendas were all there — host Vietnam even used its home-court advantage to move the FTAAP discussion a step forward.

More intriguing was what came after: the remaining TPP members turned around and signed the CPTPP, and later even the party that withdrew applied to rejoin — the multilateral road, after a long detour, still had people walking it.
Da Nang's beaches are as beautiful as a postcard, and that year's post-meeting commentary was just as direct: the table of multilateralism keeps turning whoever is missing.
◆ 37 years of taking turns, zero breakups

Over 37 years, dozens of hosts took their turn: from Canberra to Gyeongju, from suits to tang suits to video windows. Taking turns looks simple, but it's actually wisdom of mutual checks and balances — nobody gets to turn the organization into their own living room, and everybody gets a chance to be host once.

The 2025 Gyeongju meeting in South Korea even launched the APEC AI Initiative — this 37-year-old dinner party keeps adding new dishes: from free trade to digital agenda to artificial intelligence, the topic list shifts gears with the times, and the party never goes out of style.

Compare that with the fate of other multilateral mechanisms over the same period: some have stalled, some have seen waves of withdrawals, some have been declared dysfunctional — while APEC's attendance stays consistently high, with all 21 members present.
A whole basketful of twists and turns, and not one breakup — that's probably the highest praise a mechanism's resilience can get.
Cancelled, stillborn, table-flipped — APEC's history of awkward moments is its history of withstanding pressure.
An organization that can be mocked for 37 years and still sit at the head table never got there by luck.
When the next crisis comes, its résumé is already thick enough.
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.

title: Stop saying APEC only takes group photos: one card across the Asia-Pacific, faster customs, a vision out to 2040 — here's the full list of real results
summary: Stop saying APEC only takes group photos: one card across the Asia-Pacific, a paperless-trade timetable, the 2040 Vision, and the 'Shenzhen Initiative' — the first such initiative in 30 years — here's the full list of real, tangible results.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: Many people still picture APEC as just one group photo a year. Open up its actual list of results, though, and you'll find the organization's real value hidden in the details: a travel card, a set of faster customs-clearance mechanisms, and a vision written out to 2040.

These tangible results share one trait: they never make the headlines or trending lists, yet they run past you every day — the package you ordered online, your boss's business-trip visa, the import tax and fee costs on your overseas purchases all have something to do with it.
This piece lays the results out one by one; after reading it, you'll look at that group photo with different eyes.
◆ From Bogor to Putrajaya: winding the clock twice

APEC's first real result was setting an alarm clock. The 1994 Bogor Goals gave liberalization two deadlines: developed members by 2010, developing members by 2020. A 30-year review shows average import tariffs across APEC members fell from double digits back then into single digits.

In the pandemic year of 2020, the 21 members adopted the Putrajaya Vision 2040 by video: an open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful Asia-Pacific community, winding the clock again for the next twenty years; the accompanying 2021 Aotearoa Action Plan broke it into assessable blueprints.

The logic behind both clock-windings runs the same way: no binding treaty, but goals and deadlines written down in black and white for the whole Asia-Pacific to watch — the binding force of a promise comes from the spotlight.
The container-terminal cranes turning day and night are the most visible ticking of that clock.
◆ The magic of one card: the boarding pass for Asia-Pacific business

The 1999 Auckland meeting approved the APEC Business Travel Card. Businesspeople holding it don't need visas for each country, can use dedicated lanes entering and leaving participating members, and may stay up to 90 days per visit — with one card in hand, Asia-Pacific business travel gets an instant speed-up.

The card now covers nearly 20 participating members, is valid for three years and allows multiple entries. Countless foreign-trade bosses call it the boarding pass for Asia-Pacific business — as one old hand who constantly travels between China, Malaysia and Thailand puts it: the paperwork saved in a year would fill a filing cabinet.

Its essence is what APEC does best: no treaty changes, no sovereignty issues, just smoothing the process — the card is the carrier, and behind it, immigration, border control and foreign affairs departments across 21 economies are aligning their rules.
Of the travelers hurrying through Changi Airport's halls, many have this card in their pocket.
◆ Paperless trade and the digital agenda

That 1999 meeting also set a paperless-trade timetable: developed members by 2005, developing members by 2010. Electronic documents and e-customs moved forward steadily, and customs clearance went from three days of stamping to a few minutes at your fingertips.

After 2020 the agenda was upgraded again: smart customs, trade digitalization and cross-border e-commerce went into joint statements year after year; the 2026 Shenzhen meeting put cross-border data flows in the spotlight for the first time, setting up a dedicated cooperation body on digital technology and cross-border data flows.

Do the math and you'll see the value of these years: the Asia-Pacific handles nearly half of global goods trade, so every day cut from clearance time frees up an astronomical amount of capital on hundreds of billions of dollars in trade flows — paperless doesn't save paper, it saves money and time.
The blue lights blinking in data centers are the true backdrop of Asia-Pacific trade today — from fax paper to data streams, APEC has completed two blood transfusions.
◆ The connectivity blueprint: weaving three networks at once

The 2014 Beijing meeting adopted the APEC Connectivity Blueprint, weaving three networks together — infrastructure, institutions and people: building roads and ports, aligning rules, and easing people-to-people movement, with the goal of a comprehensive, multi-layered connectivity framework by 2025.

The same meeting also adopted the FTAAP roadmap — upgrading the second half of the Bogor Goals from liberalization to institution-building for a free-trade area; the 2026 Shenzhen meeting announced steady progress on the FTAAP process, renewing the roadmap twelve years later.

The ledger on the ground is even more concrete: the linking of China-Europe rail freight with Asia-Pacific shipping, progress on electronic mutual recognition, expansion of cross-border payment channels — cargo ships no longer sit stuck in port and customs clearance no longer depends on luck, all moving from vision into daily life.
Nearly half the world's goods trade runs through the Asia-Pacific, and every minute a supply chain runs smoother is hard cash.
◆ The stage for small bosses: inclusiveness isn't just a slogan

APEC has another hidden identity: the champion of small and medium enterprises — SMEs make up the overwhelming majority of businesses in the Asia-Pacific and contribute most of the jobs, with every meeting reserving a special place for them year after year.

The 2026 Shenzhen meeting carried on the tradition of the Bio-Circular-Green Economy Award: honoring small bosses who turn waste into business, with judges personally giving a thumbs-up; the SME Working Group also set up a permanent cooperation body in Shenzhen, turning support policies into industry matchmaking.

Look at the topic mix of the Shenzhen Summit's business breakout sessions: digital technology, cross-border e-commerce, green energy, SME development — half the agenda was opened for small players: the big companies set the rules, the small businesses get the benefits.
The stall owners in the market, the bakeries in the bazaar — these humble capillaries are the foundation of the Asia-Pacific economy. That's what inclusiveness really means.
◆ The Shenzhen Initiative: a first in 30 years

In Shenzhen 2026, the Chinese side announced steady progress on the FTAAP process, stronger cooperation on trade digitalization, cross-border e-commerce and smart customs, and the establishment of cooperation bodies in digital technology, cross-border data, clean energy and SMEs.

This year's outcome document, the 'Shenzhen Initiative,' is the first issued in initiative form in 30 years — leaders' meeting results used to be declarations or statements; an initiative is a more flexible, more actionable format, and you can weigh its significance for yourself.

Add US$20 million in cooperation funding, the Asia-Pacific Community Research Center, and the World Bay Area Economic Cooperation Alliance — a four-piece package landing all at once, giving the loose mechanism a purse and a brain trust for the first time.
The lights of Shenzhen's port burn all night — the anchor for the Asia-Pacific's next twenty years has been dropped.
The travel card, faster clearance, Vision 2040, the Shenzhen Initiative — APEC's real results have never been in the group photo; they're in the details.
To judge an organization, don't listen to what it says — look at what it has made faster and cheaper.
Those few things are the answer.
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.

title: Inside the Asia-Pacific shopping cart: chips, soybeans, finished cars, natural gas — what's actually in that US$15.3 trillion order book
summary: Chips, soybeans, finished cars, natural gas, parcels: open up the US$15.3 trillion annual bill and see what's in the Asia-Pacific shopping cart — every item has something to do with your life.
author: starteday 编辑部
body: APEC members import and export about US$15.3 trillion each per year, accounting for 46.7% and 46.1% of the world respectively — an astronomical figure that sounds abstract, until you break it into a shopping cart: chips, soybeans, finished cars, natural gas, parcels and plane tickets.

These 21 economies also hold half of global manufacturing: the vital point of the chip supply chain, the main artery of grain trade, the export docks for new-energy vehicles, the route maps of LNG carriers — all on this table.
This piece spreads out the order books of the 21 economies for you — every item is connected to your life.
◆ Item one, the heavy hitter: chips

The hardest currency in Asia-Pacific trade is the chip. TSMC alone makes over 90% of the world's most advanced-process chips; add Samsung's memory, Nvidia's designs and Intel's fabrication, and the vital points of the global electronics industry are mostly in APEC members' hands — a genuine strategic resource.

The relay race of the supply chain runs across both sides of the Pacific: the US provides design and equipment, Japan and Korea supply materials and memory, mainland China and Chinese Taipei handle manufacturing, packaging and testing — a single chip crosses borders a dozen-odd times on average before it goes into a phone, and the global semiconductor market tops US$600 billion a year.

So semiconductors are never a minor topic on APEC's issue list: supply-chain resilience, export controls and tariff coordination are hurdles ministerial meetings can't get around year after year — the 2025 Gyeongju meeting even launched the APEC AI Initiative, putting computing power on the agenda right alongside chips.
The wafer lifted up in white gloves is densely packed with hundreds of chips; slice it up and you have the brains of countless phones and cars.
◆ Item two: soybeans and the food basket

The second heavy hitter is agricultural products. US soybean exports are measured in tens of millions of tons annually, and crossing the Pacific they become regulars at crushing plants and feeding troughs; China is the world's largest soybean importer — one Pacific Ocean holds both the biggest grain trader and the biggest buyer.

Individual products are even livelier: Thai jasmine rice, Vietnamese coffee — Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee exporter — and Chilean cherries, riding charter flights and refrigerated ships, each topping the e-commerce platforms' New Year shopping charts.

Behind this order book lie years of negotiated tax cuts and fast-track inspections: food-security thematic meetings are held every year, and the 2026 Shenzhen meeting named them again — a stable food basket is the dinner party's most down-to-earth original intention.
The dust kicked up behind the harvester is the most primitive and most vibrant image of agricultural trade.
◆ Item three: finished cars going overseas

The third item is cars. Japan's Toyota and Korea's Hyundai-Kia have dominated the world for decades; now Chinese new-energy vehicles roll onto ro-ro ships in batches — in 2024 China exported about 5.9 million vehicles, taking the number-one spot globally, with a single ship's belly packed with thousands of cars.

Behind the car trade is a three-stage relay of finished vehicles, parts and batteries: lithium comes from Chile and Australia, batteries are made in China, whole cars are assembled in Asia, then shipped worldwide — a chain long enough to circle the globe, and no APEC member is a complete bystander.

The switch from gasoline to electric has quietly rewritten Asia-Pacific trade manifests: batteries, motors and chips have replaced engine assemblies and gearboxes, and rows of new cars waiting at ports to ship out are this era's most vivid picture of industrial change.
Rows of new cars waiting at the port to ship out are this era's most vivid picture of industrial change.
◆ Item four: the energy gas dragon

The fourth item is energy. Australia is one of the world's largest LNG exporters, with annual exports around 80 million tons, and US LNG exports have been catching up fast in recent years — shipment after shipment of gas carriers sails to Asia day and night, with China, Japan and South Korea the biggest group of buyers.
Round LNG tanks hold the energy lifeline at minus 162 degrees Celsius, and one shipment of gas can keep a city burning for days — the bulk of global LNG trade travels the Pacific routes.

The other side of the bill is transition: clean energy is a buzzword at the 2026 Shenzhen meeting, with digital technology and clean energy named side by side as new fields for cooperation bodies — the age of the gas dragon is switching tracks.
From coal to gas to wind, solar and storage, the manifest of Asia-Pacific energy trade is a microcosm of human energy history.
◆ Item five: the parcel deluge

The fifth item is closest to you and me: parcels. Cross-border e-commerce has broken Asia-Pacific trade out of shipping containers into delivery boxes — fully managed, overseas warehouses, semi-managed, with a new model every year — China's annual cross-border e-commerce trade has long surpassed the trillion-yuan mark and still grows by double digits year after year.

Another angle is even more staggering: thousands of cargo flights cross the Pacific every day, and the sorting belts in airport cargo terminals spin nonstop — small parcels have pieced together a trillion-dollar business.

The rulebook underpinning this business was also laid by APEC: cross-border e-commerce, smart customs and trade digitalization have gone into leaders' meeting documents year after year, and the 2026 Shenzhen Initiative added another layer of official endorsement.
In the time it takes a delivery van to pull over and unload, hundreds of thousands of cross-border parcels may be in the air over the Asia-Pacific.
◆ Item six: people and services

The last item is invisible but the most valuable: people and services. Tourists, international students and business travelers hold up half the sky of Asia-Pacific service trade — in 2019, before the pandemic, international passenger numbers in the Asia-Pacific were counted in the hundreds of millions, and now the airport halls are lined up again.

The bill for services trade comes in more varieties: education abroad, medical treatment, exhibitions, software outsourcing, digital content — a software subscription costing the price of a milk tea can be a cross-border services transaction, completed at your fingertips with no customs form needed.

This is also APEC's area of expertise: the Business Travel Card, study-abroad facilitation, and alignment of people-movement policies — after goods flow freely across the world, people do too, and that's exactly what the connectivity blueprint is about.
This is the most human chapter in APEC's connectivity blueprint, and the only item the shopping cart can't hold.
Chips, soybeans, finished cars, natural gas, parcels and people — six items that piece together the US$15.3 trillion annual bill.
Understand the Asia-Pacific's shopping cart and you understand the engine of the global economy.
Next time you scroll past an APEC group photo, the word on your lips won't be 'photo op' — it'll be 'ledger.'
This article draws on public reports from the APEC official website and Xinhua.
